title: Prediction Record
description: One prediction, or one abstention, together with the evidence that is claimed to support it. This is the subject the standards evaluate: not a model, not a repository, but a single output and what stands behind it. Four quantities that are routinely confused are kept structurally apart here — `output.probability` is the probability of the event, `confidence.tier` is how much weight to put on that number, `edge.value` is the difference from a market reference, and `expectedValue.value` is a monetary quantity. No field can play two of those roles, so conflating them is a schema error rather than a matter of prose.

schemaVersion.description: The record schema version this document claims to follow. Versioned independently of the standards series so a record format change and a rule change are never mistaken for each other.

seriesId.description: Optional. Links successive predictions about the same subject so a silent change of methodology between them can be detected. Without it, each record is an island and 'the method changed and nobody said so' is unobservable.

expiresAt.description: When this prediction stops being usable. Required for predictions and forbidden for abstentions, which the evaluator enforces because the schema's conditional vocabulary cannot. A prediction with no expiry is one that will still be quoted after its inputs are meaningless.

timestamp.description: ISO-8601 instant with an explicit offset. A local time without an offset is ambiguous, and every staleness and expiry judgement in this system is arithmetic on these values.

duration.description: ISO-8601 duration, e.g. P7D or PT12H.

probability.description: A probability, in the unit interval. Not a percentage, not a score, not a confidence.

subject.description: What is being predicted. A probability with no resolvable event attached is not a prediction about anything — this block is what makes the number falsifiable.

outcomeDefinition.description: The precise condition that counts as the event occurring. This is where 'it will rain tomorrow' becomes something two people cannot argue about after the fact.

resolutionSource.description: Who or what settles the outcome.

falsifiability.description: The producer's declaration that the outcome named above was still open when this record was generated. Introduced in record schema 1.1.0 and optional in the document shape, so a 1.0.0 record remains well-formed; `falsifiability.declared` requires it from 1.1.0 onward and reports not-evaluated below that (ADR 0008). A record whose resolution target was already computed cannot be wrong, and Adoptions #2 and #3 both produced one that satisfied every other rule in this pack.

undeterminedAtGeneration.description: True when the resolution target was not determined by the act or state that produced this prediction. False is a legitimate thing to say and makes the artifact something other than a prediction, so it is recorded rather than forbidden — and it fails the rule instead of failing the schema.

basis.description: Why the outcome was still open. What has to happen before the resolution source can answer, in enough detail that a reviewer can disagree.

methodology.description: How the number was produced. Named and versioned so that a change between two predictions in a series is visible rather than silent.

changedFromPrevious.description: Whether this record's method differs from the previous record in its series. Absent means false. Declaring the change is the whole requirement; nothing here forbids changing methods.

changeNote.description: What changed and why. Required by the evaluator when changedFromPrevious is true.

output.description: The prediction itself, or the refusal to make one. Exactly one of the two variants applies, and each forbids the other's fields: an abstention carrying a probability is not an abstention, and a prediction carrying the abstention statement is a contradiction. Abstention is a first-class output here, not an error state — a well-formed abstention is a valid, supported result.

probabilityStated.description: The probability as displayed, if it is displayed with trailing zeros that JSON cannot preserve — '0.60' parses as 0.6 and the stated precision is lost. Supply it when precision matters; the false-precision check reads it in preference to the number.

statement.description: Fixed wording, reproduced from the source specification. Fixed so that abstention is recognisable mechanically and cannot be softened into something that reads like a weak prediction.

reasons.description: Why no prediction is being made. At least one, because an unexplained abstention cannot be acted on or reviewed.

interval.description: The uncertainty around the point estimate. Required for every prediction: a bare number claims a precision it does not have, and the interval is what stops a 0.62 from being read as exact.

level.description: Interval level, strictly between 0 and 1 — 0.9 for a 90% interval. Exactly 0 or 1 describes no interval anyone can act on.

method.description: How the interval was derived, e.g. 'bootstrap, 2000 resamples'.

baseline.description: The reference probability this prediction should be read against — the base rate, the naive forecast, the status quo. Either give it, or say plainly that there isn't one and why. A prediction with no reference point cannot be judged as better or worse than knowing nothing.

basis.description: What the baseline is a rate of, and over what population and period.

data.description: The evidence base: how much, how complete, how fresh, and how the awkward observations were treated.

unit.description: What is being counted — matches, days, filings. A bare n is uninterpretable.

basis.description: Which observations these are, and why they are the relevant ones.

justification.description: Why a sample below the project's minimum is nonetheless sufficient here. Read by the evaluator only when n falls short.

knownGaps.description: Gaps that are known and judged not to be decisive. May be empty; an empty array is a claim, not a silence.

criticalMissing.description: Missing information that bears materially on the outcome. Non-empty on a prediction demands a justification below, or the honest answer is abstention.

justification.description: Why a prediction is defensible despite the critical gaps listed. Required by the evaluator when criticalMissing is non-empty on a prediction.

dataAsOf.description: The instant the underlying data describes — not when it was fetched. Those differ, and the difference is where staleness hides.

freshnessWindow.description: How long this data stays usable for this kind of prediction. Falls back to the project's default when absent.

stalenessAccounted.description: How the age of the data was allowed for — a widened interval, a decayed weight, a discount. Required by the evaluator once the data is older than its window. Using stale data is permitted; using it as though it were fresh is not.

assessed.description: Whether outliers were looked for at all. False is an admission, not a pass.

handling.description: What was done with them, and why that is not just discarding inconvenient observations. Required by the evaluator when detected is true.

regime.description: Whether the world this model learned from is still the world being predicted. A model can be sound and its training regime gone.

accountedFor.description: How the change was handled. Required by the evaluator when changeDetected is true.

ensemble.description: The individual models behind the number, when there is more than one. Present so that disagreement is visible and exclusions are answerable: a model dropped without a stated reason is indistinguishable from a model dropped for giving the wrong answer.

method.description: How member probabilities became the reported one, e.g. 'weighted-mean' or 'median'.

spread.description: Highest member probability minus lowest. The evaluator recomputes this from the members; a stated spread that disagrees with them is a finding.

declared.description: Whether the disagreement is being surfaced as material. Required to be true once the spread exceeds the project's threshold.

note.description: What the disagreement means for this prediction. Required by the evaluator alongside declared.

excluded.description: Models considered and left out. Every exclusion carries a reason — this is the anti-cherry-picking mechanism, and it is deliberately weak assurance: it catches the exclusions that were disclosed, never the ones that were never mentioned.

reason.description: Why it was excluded, in terms that do not reduce to 'it disagreed'.

market.description: The market or reference expectation this prediction is measured against, when one exists. Either give it, or say there isn't one and why — 'when relevant' is a judgement the record must state rather than leave to inference.

impliedProbability.description: The market's probability for this outcome, after vig removal where raw prices are given.

raw.description: The quoted prices across every outcome of the market. Supplying them is what lets the evaluator recompute the overround and check the de-vigging rather than take it on trust.

vig.description: The bookmaker's margin and what was done about it. Raw prices across a market sum to more than 1; treating them as probabilities without removing that excess overstates every outcome, and an edge computed against them is an artefact of the margin.

method.description: `proportional` scales every implied probability by the overround; `power` and `shin` distribute it unevenly to counter favourite-longshot bias; `none-needed` claims the prices already sum to 1. The evaluator recomputes proportional in full and checks only the presence of the others, which its assurance note states plainly.

overround.description: Sum of raw implied probabilities minus 1. Recomputed by the evaluator when raw prices are supplied.

edge.description: How far this prediction departs from the market reference. Not a probability and not a monetary value: a signed difference between two probabilities. Requires a market to have been given — an edge over nothing is not an edge.

basis.description: How it was computed. The evaluator recomputes the standard basis and compares.

materialityNote.description: Why an edge this small is nonetheless meaningful. Required by the evaluator when the edge falls below the project's materiality threshold — the answer to 'a tiny modeled difference called meaningful without justification'.

expectedValue.description: A monetary quantity, in currency units, not a probability and not an edge. Requires a stake and a payout: without them there is no wager to have an expected value, and a number presented as EV is just a probability wearing a different name.

payout.description: Total returned on a win, stake included.

confidence.description: How much weight to put on the probability — a statement about the strength of the evidence, not about the event. Categorical on purpose: a numeric confidence invites arithmetic against the probability, and the two are not the same quantity. The evaluator rejects a tier that is merely a number wearing a label.

vocabularyRef.description: Where the tier's definition lives: `policy` for the project's declared vocabulary, `inline` for one carried in this record.

vocabulary.description: The tiers and their definitions, when vocabularyRef is `inline`.

calibration.description: Whether this methodology's stated probabilities have been checked against outcomes, and if so, how. A claim of calibration is a claim about a measurement someone performed; this block is where that measurement is named, and the evaluator will not accept a score without one.

dataset.description: What it was measured on, including the period. A calibration measured on the data the model was fitted to is not a calibration.

score.description: The measured result. Forbidden when measured is false — a score with no measurement behind it is the fabrication this pack exists to prevent.

provenance.description: Where this record and its inputs came from, and whether it is a historical reconstruction. The historical block is what makes lookahead detectable: a prediction dated to the past that draws on data from after that date is not a prediction, it is a memory.

asOf.description: The instant this source's content describes. Compared against the information cutoff on historical records.

isHistorical.description: True when this record reconstructs a prediction as it would have been made at an earlier time — for backtesting or for measuring calibration.

informationCutoff.description: The instant beyond which no information was permitted to inform this prediction. Required by the evaluator when isHistorical is true; every data source must be as-of at or before it.
